title: Practice: mean and range from grouped data
intro: Nine questions. A calculator is fine here — the skill is setting out the table correctly.

questions.prompt: Quick-fire: the midpoint of each class.
questions.explanation: Add the two boundaries and halve: $\frac{150 + 155}{2} = 152.5$.

questions.prompt: Complete the table for the heights of 30 plants.
hints: Midpoint first, then multiply by the frequency in the same row.
questions.explanation: Midpoints 15, 25, 35, 45. Products 60, 200, 385, 315, which total 960. The estimated mean is $960 \div 30 = 32$ cm.

questions.prompt: Estimate the mean one step at a time.

steps.prompt: What is the midpoint of the class $125 \le m < 130$?
Work out $\Sigma fx$. (The products are 612.5, 2040, 1722.5, 550 and 285.)
Estimate the mean mass, in grams.
steps.hint: Divide $\Sigma fx$ by the total frequency, 40.

questions.explanation: $\Sigma fx = 5210$ and $\Sigma f = 40$, so the estimated mean is $130.25$ g — sensibly near the two biggest classes.

questions.prompt: Students' distances from school: $0 \le d < 1$: 10, $\;1 \le d < 2$: 15, $\;2 \le d < 3$: 7, $\;3 \le d < 4$: 2, $\;4 \le d < 5$: 1. Estimate the mean distance, to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: $\Sigma fx = 56.5$ and $\Sigma f = 35$, so the mean $\approx 56.5 \div 35 = 1.61$ km.

questions.prompt: For the same students, estimate the range of distances.
hints: Upper boundary of the last class minus the lower boundary of the first.
questions.explanation: $5 - 0 = 5$ km. It is an estimate — the real furthest and nearest students could be closer together than this.

questions.prompt: The masses of 40 oranges all lie between 120 g and 145 g. Sarah thinks the mean is about 115 g and Freddie thinks it is over 140 g. Why are both wrong?

options.text: 115 g is below every orange, and over 140 g would need nearly every orange in the top class
The mean must be exactly the middle of the range, 132.5 g
You cannot find a mean from grouped data
The mean is always in the modal class

hints: Where must the mean of a set of numbers always lie?
questions.explanation: A mean always lies between the smallest and largest values. 115 g is smaller than every orange. Only 2 of the 40 oranges are over 140 g, so the mean cannot be that high. (b and d sound plausible but are not rules.)

questions.prompt: Why are the mean and range from a grouped table only **estimates**? Select all that apply.

options.text: We do not know the exact values inside each class
Using the midpoint assumes every value is in the middle of its class
The range uses the class boundaries, which may not be real values

hints: Think about what information is lost when data is grouped.
questions.explanation: Grouping throws away the exact values, so the midpoint and the boundaries are stand-ins. Calculator rounding has nothing to do with it.
$\Sigma fx = 15\,700$ and $\Sigma f = 500$, so the mean $\approx 31.4$ years.

questions.prompt: The first three classes of the plant data are shown. The last class, $40 \le h < 50$, should make the total frequency **30**. Set it correctly.
questions.explanation: $30 - 23 = 7$. With all four classes in place the estimated mean is 32 cm.
